extracted.intended_audience: writers, literature students, and general readers interested in narrative theory and character roles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and definitional criteria for identifying, classifying, and depicting protagonists in fiction and drama, including types (hero, antihero, tragic hero, villain protagonist, supporting/false protagonists) and their narrative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main character / narrative centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist is the main character of a story. The protagonist is the character whose fate is most closely followed by the reader or audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the primary organizing figure of the narrative; in single-character stories the terms protagonist and main protagonist are often interchangeable. Examples referenced: Hamlet, Romeo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency / decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist makes key decisions that affect the plot, primarily influencing the story and propelling it forward, and is often the character who faces the most significant obstacles and choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful test for protagonist status is whose decisions move the plot; protagonists commonly encounter pivotal choices that determine narrative direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition by antagonist / conflict-driven development
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist is opposed by the antagonist. The antagonist provides obstacles and complications and creates conflicts that test the protagonist, revealing the strengths and weaknesses of the protagonist's character, and having the protagonist develop as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict with an antagonist is a core mechanism for revealing character and producing development. Assess protagonists by how conflict exposes their traits and prompts growth or change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero / heroine (conventional heroic protagonist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero (masculine) or heroine (feminine) protagonist is typically admired for their achievements and noble qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits include strength, courage, virtuousness, and honor; considered the "good guys" of the narrative. Examples given: Superman, Katniss Everdeen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antihero (protagonist lacking conventional heroic qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: An antihero or antiheroine is a main character who lacks conventional heroic qualities and attributes such as idealism, courage, and morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiheroes can still be protagonists despite failing heroic norms. Examples include Holden Caulfield, Scarlett O'Hara, Jay Gatsby.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero (protagonist of a tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic hero is the protagonist of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often characterized by a fall resulting from flaw or circumstance; examples include Oedipus and Prince Hamlet. (Page references the tragic-hero type without extensive formal criteria.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Main protagonist in multi-protagonist/ensemble narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: In narratives with multiple protagonists (ensemble casts or multi-perspective storytelling), one character is often identified as the main protagonist—typically the character who receives the greatest narrative focus and plays the most significant role in advancing the central plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main-protagonist status is defined by narrative centrality rather than morality; prominence may shift or be shared over time. The distinction matters mainly in multi-protagonist works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Villain protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: A villain protagonist is a protagonist who is a villain, driving the story forward regardless of the evil qualities the main character has.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Villain-protagonist traits can include cruelty, maliciousness, and wickedness. Examples: Humbert Humbert (Lolita), Richard III, Frank Underwood, Tony Soprano, Light Yagami, Walter White.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting protagonist (peripheral/observer viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: A supporting protagonist appears when the story is told from the perspective of a character who appears to be minor and may be more peripheral from the main events of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting protagonists may narrate while viewing another character as the main influence on the plot; example given: Nick Carraway in The Great Gatsby.

rubrics_metrics.name: False protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: A false protagonist is a character who may seem to be the protagonist but then may disappear unexpectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a narrative device to subvert audience expectations; example: Marion in Hitchcock's Psycho.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-human protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonists are not always human; a story's protagonist can be non-human (e.g., animals) or collective characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hazel and the anthropomorphised rabbits in Watership Down; assess protagonisthood by narrative focus and agency, not species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot-specific protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story contains a subplot, or is a narrative made up of several stories, then each subplot may have its own protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating protagonists in complex narratives, identify protagonists at the subplot level as well as for the central plot—each can have its own arc and focal character.
